title: Fire Officer I
summary: Company-officer skills: size-up, initial radio report, assignments, accountability, risk, coaching, documentation, and transfer of command.

skills.title: Initial Radio Report
skills.summary: From the seat, paint a picture: occupancy, conditions, actions, strategy, and what you need next — in a format later units can use.
skills.whyItMatters: The rest of the incident will copy your first 20 seconds. A vague ‘we have fire showing’ wastes staffing.
learningPoints: Say what you see: building, occupancy, fire/smoke location and extent, obvious life hazard.
Say what you are doing: investigation, attack, command mode.
Say what you need: next companies, water, special resources.
Leave room for the next unit’s assignment.
Department format wins over any textbook script.
beforeYouDo: Practice with photos — not just live chaos.

terminology.meaning: The first structured on-scene transmission that orients the response.
Investigating, fast-attack, or command from a fixed position — per local ICS habits.

safetyNotes: Do not commit crews in the report you have not actually assigned.
If you are wrong, correct it on the next transmission — do not defend a bad picture.

drill.objective: Deliver a complete initial radio report from an arrival image in 20–30 seconds, then assign the first arriving engine.
drill.equipment: Arrival images, timer, training radio or partner.
drill.setup: Training talkgroup. One person scores missing elements.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Recite your department template from memory.
debrief: What does later-arriving Truck need to hear?

15.title: 15-minute photo reps
15.instructions: Six images: house, garden apartment, strip mall, car, dumpster, nothing showing. 25 seconds each.
debrief: Did you declare a strategy?

30.title: 30-minute evolving arrival
30.instructions: Give the IRR, then a 60-second later update after a condition card (victim at window / basement / wires down).
debrief: When do you move from fast-attack to a command post?

readinessQuestions.q: An initial radio report should help later units:
choices: Know occupancy, conditions, your actions, and where to go/work
Stay on the original dispatch until they see it themselves
readinessQuestions.why: It is a working picture, not a vibe.

readinessQuestions.q: If your first report was wrong:
choices: Correct it as soon as you know — pride is not a strategy
readinessQuestions.why: Bad information kills.

readinessQuestions.q: ‘Fire showing’ without location or occupancy:
choices: Is incomplete — where, what building, and what are you doing?
readinessQuestions.why: Show the problem, not just the color of the smoke.

skills.title: Size-Up and Risk
skills.summary: Build a usable picture: life hazard, fire location, building, access, water, and what would change your mind.
skills.whyItMatters: Strategy without size-up is a guess with a radio.
learningPoints: A 360 (or a delegated 360) is how you stop lying to yourself about the D side.
Life hazard drives risk. Vacant vs occupied is not a vibe — verify.
Name the construction/collapse problem in plain language.
Size-up continues after arrival. The fire gets a vote.

terminology.meaning: A complete walk-around or equivalent view of all sides.
What we are willing to risk, for whom, given what we know.

safetyNotes: Do not send a member on a solo 360 into an unseen hazard without a plan.
Wires, holes, and dogs are size-up items too.

drill.objective: From an occupancy, complete a size-up that names life hazard, fire location, building concerns, water, and a go/hold/no-go for interior.
drill.equipment: Photos or a real drill site, radio, notepad.
drill.setup: If using a real building, stay outside unless it is a training burn under instructors.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: List the size-up factors you will not skip even when the fire looks ‘easy.’
debrief: What would a basement change?

15.title: 15-minute 360 tabletop
15.instructions: Image set missing the D side until you ask. Practice requesting the 360.
debrief: Who did you send?

30.title: 30-minute risk drill
30.instructions: Three occupancies: occupied night residential, vacant commercial, and a working fire with a report of a trapped person. State risk and what new info would change it.
debrief: When do we switch to defensive?

readinessQuestions.q: A missing 360 most often hides:
choices: Fire in the rear, basement involvement, or a victim at the back
readinessQuestions.why: The D side is where surprises live.

readinessQuestions.q: Risk/benefit should be stated in terms of:
choices: How it will look on video
Who is savable, what the building is doing, and what we can actually staff
readinessQuestions.why: It is a decision, not a slogan.

readinessQuestions.q: Size-up after water on the fire:
choices: Continues — conditions and remaining risk change
Should be deleted from the radio
readinessQuestions.why: The incident is not static.

skills.title: Strategy and Tactics
skills.summary: Pick a strategy you can staff, assign tactics that match it, and change both when the fire tells you to.
skills.whyItMatters: Offensive tactics under a defensive strategy (or the reverse) is how companies get stretched into bad air.
learningPoints: Strategy is the overall plan (e.g., offensive interior vs defensive exterior) — local terms vary.
Tactics are the assigned tasks that make the strategy real.
If you do not have water, staffing, or a building that will take people, the strategy is a wish.
Announce strategy so later units do not freelance the opposite.
beforeYouDo: A fire problem with a staffing limit.

terminology.meaning: The overall approach to the incident.
The specific assignments that implement the strategy.

safetyNotes: Do not keep an interior strategy out of stubbornness when the building has declared otherwise.
Transitional attack is a tactic with rules — not a loophole to skip size-up.

drill.objective: State a strategy, give three tactical assignments, then change strategy when a condition card drops.
drill.equipment: Scenario cards, radios, optional board for ICS chart.
drill.setup: Tabletop. Cap staffing at a realistic first-alarm.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Define strategy vs tactics using one house fire.
debrief: What do we tell the second engine?

15.title: 15-minute first alarm
15.instructions: Assign engine, truck, and later engine. Keep it inside the strategy.
debrief: Where is water coming from?

30.title: 30-minute change drill
30.instructions: Two condition changes (collapse warning / victim / water loss). Show the radio announcement of the new strategy.
debrief: Who is still inside?

readinessQuestions.q: If strategy is defensive, an interior search assignment:
choices: Must be justified by a specific savable life and a plan — not autopilot
readinessQuestions.why: Match tactics to strategy unless you are making a deliberate, staffed exception.

readinessQuestions.q: The second-due company should learn the strategy from:
readinessQuestions.why: Say it.

readinessQuestions.q: A strategy change requires:
choices: A reason, an announcement, and accountability for crews already committed
readinessQuestions.why: People are already in motion.

skills.title: Assignments and Accountability
skills.summary: Every member has a task, a location, and a way to be counted — especially when the plan changes.
skills.whyItMatters: Unassigned firefighters invent jobs in the worst air. Unaccounted firefighters become Maydays with no last location.
learningPoints: Closed-loop assignments: they repeat it back.
Know who is inside, doing what, on which hoseline or search.
PAR is a tool, not a ritual — use it when the incident needs it.
Freelancers are an officer problem, not a personality quirk.

terminology.meaning: Personnel accountability report — a roll-call of assigned crews.
How many assignments one officer can actually track.

safetyNotes: If you cannot name where a crew is, you do not have command of them.
Accountability during a Mayday is how RIT finds a starting point.

drill.objective: Assign a first-alarm, track locations on a simple chart, then run a PAR after a strategy change.
drill.equipment: Helmet shields or name cards, board, radios.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: From a riding list, give every member a job in 60 seconds.
debrief: Who is still in the cab?

15.title: 15-minute tracking
15.instructions: Move crews through assignments. Officer must point to each crew’s location on demand.
commonMistakes: Lost a crew on the board
debrief: Where is the backup line crew?

30.title: 30-minute PAR
30.instructions: Working fire, then a collapse or Mayday inject. PAR in department format. Identify who is missing on purpose.
commonMistakes: Skipping PAR because it is awkward
debrief: What did RIT get from us?

readinessQuestions.q: An unassigned firefighter on the fireground should be:
choices: Given a job or staged — not left to freelance
Sent to the roof by default
readinessQuestions.why: Initiative without an assignment is how extra holes and extra victims appear.

readinessQuestions.q: If you cannot say where a crew is:
choices: It is fine if they have a radio
You have an accountability problem now
readinessQuestions.why: Location is the product.

readinessQuestions.q: PAR is most useful:
choices: When something changed or someone may be missing
readinessQuestions.why: It is a check against reality.

skills.title: Transfer of Command
skills.summary: Hand off a compact brief: situation, strategy, assignments, accountability, resources, hazards, and immediate needs.
skills.whyItMatters: A bad transfer creates two commanders and zero accountability.
learningPoints: Face-to-face when you can. Radio when you must.
The incoming officer confirms they have command — on the air.
Do not dump a novel. Dump the picture.
Stay and help unless you are reassigned.
beforeYouDo: A working-fire tabletop already in progress.
safetyNotes: Do not walk away before the other person actually has it.
If crews are in trouble, that is the first sentence, not the last.

practiceResources.label: Fire Instructor I — briefing
practiceResources.note: Clear briefings transfer to the fireground too.

drill.objective: Give a 45-second command transfer brief, then the incoming IC repeats the critical pieces on the radio.
drill.equipment: Scenario in progress, two officers, radios, worksheet.
drill.setup: Tabletop. Incoming IC may ask two questions only.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: List the seven items that must be in the brief.
debrief: What if a crew is missing?

15.title: 15-minute briefs
15.instructions: Three incidents, three transfers. Score missing pieces.
debrief: Did the new IC actually own it?

30.title: 30-minute messy transfer
30.instructions: Mayday in progress during the handshake. Practice not dropping either ball.
debrief: Who is IC during the Mayday?

readinessQuestions.q: Command has transferred when:
choices: The incoming officer acknowledges command per department practice
readinessQuestions.why: Arrival is not transfer.

readinessQuestions.q: The brief should start with:
choices: Life hazards / urgent problems, then strategy and assignments
readinessQuestions.why: Lead with what can kill people in the next minute.

readinessQuestions.q: After transfer you should:
choices: Remain available as assigned — you still have crew knowledge
Countermand the new IC on the radio
readinessQuestions.why: You are still a resource.

skills.title: Coaching and Crew Performance
skills.summary: Correct a specific behavior with a private, factual conversation: what you saw, the standard, the impact, and the follow-up.
skills.whyItMatters: Officers who only yell in the bay never fix the thing that will hurt someone at 3 a.m.
learningPoints: Public praise, private correction — as a default.
Behavior, not identity. ‘You skipped the 360’ not ‘you’re lazy.’
Tie it to a standard (SOP, safety, crew agreement).
Document when policy says to. Do not ambush with a file the person never saw.
If it is a policy/HR issue, use the actual process — do not freelance discipline.

terminology.meaning: Formal steps when coaching is not enough — follow policy.

safetyNotes: Safety violations may require immediate stop, then the conversation.
Do not humiliate people. It creates silent crews.

drill.objective: Run a 4-minute coaching conversation on a specific fireground miss, then agree on one observable next rep.
drill.equipment: Role-play cards, quiet room, optional note template.
drill.setup: No real personnel files. Fiction only.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Write the four parts: observed, standard, impact, ask.
debrief: Where would this happen on shift?

15.title: 15-minute role-play
15.instructions: Two rounds: skipped accountability tag, then a rude public complaint. Switch roles.
debrief: What is the follow-up date?

30.title: 30-minute conflict
30.instructions: Two members snapping at each other. Officer facilitates facts, expectations, and a boundary. Know when to escalate to the chief/HR path.
debrief: Is this coaching or a formal complaint?

readinessQuestions.q: The most useful coaching statement is:
choices: A specific behavior plus the standard plus the effect on the crew
readinessQuestions.why: People can fix what they can see.

readinessQuestions.q: Correcting a safety issue in front of the whole company:
choices: May be required to stop the danger — then take the teaching private
readinessQuestions.why: Stop the harm, then teach.

readinessQuestions.q: If the issue is harassment or a policy violation beyond your authority:
choices: Follow department reporting rules — do not bury it in ‘coaching’
Tell them to get over it
readinessQuestions.why: Officers are a reporting path, not a lid.

officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Department HR / discipline / workplace SOP
officialSources.scope: What you may document and when you must escalate are local legal/HR rules.

skills.title: Incident Documentation
skills.summary: Write what happened in objective language: times, decisions, people (as required), and follow-up — without creative writing.
skills.whyItMatters: The report is how the organization learns, defends, and improves. A sloppy narrative becomes the official story.
learningPoints: Facts vs opinions. Label them if you must include both.
Chronology helps. So do names/units per policy.
Do not put patient identifiers in a training log — and follow HIPAA/privacy on real EMS reports.
If you changed strategy, say why in plain language.
Complete required fields. ‘See narrative’ is not a strategy for checkboxes.
beforeYouDo: A de-identified sample report or a fictional incident.

terminology.meaning: What was observed and done, not a novel about motives.

safetyNotes: Training documentation is not an official NFIRS record. Do not treat FireOpsSim notes as the department system of record.
Never enter protected health information into FireOpsSim.

drill.objective: Edit a messy de-identified narrative into a clear chronology with decisions and follow-up, then list three missing official-system fields you would still need on a real report.
drill.equipment: Sample narrative (fiction), timer, department field list if available.
drill.setup: No real incident data, no patient names.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Strike opinions from a bad paragraph.
debrief: What is still missing?

15.title: 15-minute rewrite
15.instructions: Turn a 200-word rant into a 120-word chronology.
debrief: Would a later investigator understand the strategy change?

30.title: 30-minute complete package
30.instructions: Narrative plus a list of notifications (investigation, exposure, injury) that policy might require — as a checklist, not a filing.
debrief: Where does this actually get entered on shift?

readinessQuestions.q: A good company-officer narrative emphasizes:
choices: Observable conditions, actions, times, and decisions
readinessQuestions.why: The next reader was not there.

readinessQuestions.q: Protected health information belongs:
choices: In the official EMS/hospital system per law and agency rules — not in this training product
readinessQuestions.why: FireOpsSim is not a PCR.

readinessQuestions.q: If you are unsure whether an injury/exposure must be reported:
choices: Follow department occupational-reporting rules — do not guess it away
readinessQuestions.why: Reporting paths exist for a reason.

skills.title: Risk Management
skills.summary: Name the risk, reduce it if you can, refuse what you cannot staff, and take care of the crew after the work.
skills.whyItMatters: Company officers are the last people who can still say ‘we are not doing that’ before someone pays.
learningPoints: Risk to firefighters must buy something: savable life, or a building that still has a reason.
Rehab, air, and rotation are risk controls, not comforts.
Near-misses are free lessons if you catch them.
Health/exposure reporting is part of the job, not weakness.
beforeYouDo: NIOSH mindset: what has killed officers’ crews before.

terminology.meaning: Atmosphere immediately dangerous to life and health — SCBA and staffing rules apply.
Rest, cooling/warming, medical watch, hydration — a control measure.

safetyNotes: Do not mock members for sitting in rehab.
Cancer and cardiac events are occupational realities — policy exists; use it.

drill.objective: For three scenarios, state the risk, the control, and the condition that would make you refuse or withdraw.
drill.equipment: Scenario cards, optional rehab kit for a practical piece.
drill.setup: Include one heat-stress and one vacant-building problem.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Name five firefighter killers that are not ‘the fire.’
debrief: What does NIOSH keep repeating?

15.title: 15-minute go/no-go
15.instructions: Occupied vs vacant vs no water. Officer states the line they will not cross.
debrief: What did we still not know?

30.title: 30-minute company risk
30.instructions: Working fire tabletop plus a rehab rotation and an exposure/near-miss report talk-through.
debrief: Who is watching the crew medically?

readinessQuestions.q: Risking firefighters in a well-involved vacant with no reported life hazard:
choices: Should be hard to justify — match risk to benefit
Is a good training opportunity during the fire
readinessQuestions.why: Buildings can be written off. People cannot.

readinessQuestions.q: Rehab is:
choices: A union issue unrelated to safety
readinessQuestions.why: Cardiac events happen after the fire too.

readinessQuestions.q: A near-miss should be:
choices: Captured through the department process so the next crew does not repeat it
readinessQuestions.why: Free lessons expire if you bury them.

skills.title: After-Action Review
skills.summary: Run a short, blame-light review: what we intended, what happened, why, what to keep, and one change.
skills.whyItMatters: If the only review is yelling, the crew learns to hide. If there is no review, the next fire is a repeat.
learningPoints: Do it close to the event while facts are fresh — and when people can hear.
Start with the plan vs the result.
Let the nozzle talk before the officer speech.
One or two takeaways beat twenty.
Serious policy/safety issues may need a separate official process.
beforeYouDo: A recent training scenario, not a real sensitive personnel case.

terminology.meaning: A structured conversation about a just-completed event.

safetyNotes: Do not use the AAR to humiliate.
If someone is injured or a Mayday occurred, follow official investigation rules — this drill is not that process.

drill.objective: Facilitate a 10-minute AAR after a drill using intended vs actual, plus one sustain and one improve.
drill.equipment: Just-finished skill (hose, radio, search), timer, whiteboard optional.
drill.setup: Everyone stands unless rehab is needed. Officer facilitates, does not monopolize.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Write the four AAR questions on a card and stick to them.
debrief: When do we not AAR in the street?

15.title: 15-minute facilitated AAR
15.instructions: After a 10-minute hose drill, run the AAR. Lowest-rank speaks first.
debrief: What will we actually change tomorrow?

30.title: 30-minute train-the-facilitator
30.instructions: Two AARs: one after a win, one after a mess. Practice stopping blame and extracting a system fix.
debrief: Does this need a formal report instead?

readinessQuestions.q: The first useful AAR comparison is:
choices: Intended plan vs what actually happened
readinessQuestions.why: Reality vs plan.

readinessQuestions.q: If a member made a dangerous mistake, the AAR should:
choices: Address the action and the system that allowed it — not a public shaming session
readinessQuestions.why: Fix the thing. Keep the human usable.

readinessQuestions.q: A 40-item improvement list:
choices: Usually means nothing will change — pick one or two
readinessQuestions.why: Focus beats catalogs.
